title: Gabriel's Horn
subject: Analysis
statement: Rotating the curve y = 1/x for x ≥ 1 about the x-axis gives a solid of finite volume whose surface has infinite area.
short: A horn that holds a finite amount of paint has an inner surface that no finite amount of paint could cover.
long: Torricelli's horn, studied in the seventeenth century, is the surface swept out by 1/x beyond x = 1. Its cross-sections shrink fast enough that the enclosed volume is just π, but the circumference of each slice shrinks only like 1/x, and the harmonic integral diverges. The apparent contradiction dissolves once you notice that painting the inside requires a layer of nonzero thickness, which would need infinitely much paint.
proof: V=\pi\int_1^\infty x^{-2}dx=\pi. Since \sqrt{1+x^{-4}}\ge1, comparison gives A\ge2\pi\int_1^\infty dx/x=\infty.
consequence: It sharpens the distinction between a region's volume and the area of its boundary, and is the classic caution against 'fill it but cannot paint it' reasoning in analysis.

title: The Coastline Paradox
subject: Recreational Mathematics
statement: A coastline has no well-defined length: the shorter your ruler, the longer the measured boundary becomes.
short: Measure Britain with a kilometre stick or a metre stick and you get two different, equally defensible answers.
long: Lewis Fry Richardson noticed that mapmakers using different ruler lengths produced wildly different coastline totals, and the discrepancy did not settle down as the ruler shrank. Mandelbrot later read this as evidence that a coastline is fractal-like: its detail keeps reappearing at every magnification. The measured length therefore depends on the resolution of the measurement, and a dimension larger than one is needed to describe how fast it grows.
proof: If each step of size \varepsilon exposes a fixed amount of new zigzag, the number of steps scales like \varepsilon^{-D} with D>1, so L(\varepsilon)=N(\varepsilon)\varepsilon\sim C\varepsilon^{1-D}\to\infty.
consequence: It motivated fractal dimension and matters whenever a measured quantity depends on resolution, from tortuous borders to turbulent flow and digital image analysis.

title: Benford's Law
subject: Statistics
statement: In many naturally occurring datasets, the leading digit is 1 about 30% of the time and 9 only about 5%.
short: Numbers in the wild are not evenly spread: small leading digits turn up far more often than large ones.
long: Frank Benford noticed in 1938 that tables of logarithms were dirtier at the front pages, and that the same bias recurred in river lengths, populations and physical constants. The reason is scale invariance: data spanning many orders of magnitude look much the same after multiplying by a constant, which forces the fractional parts of their base-10 logarithms to be uniform. That yields the logarithmic probabilities, with 1 taking nearly a third of all leading positions.
proof: Scale invariance forces the fractional parts of \log_{10}x to be uniform. The leading digit is d exactly when \{\log_{10}x\}\in[\log_{10}d,\log_{10}(d+1)), an interval of length \log_{10}(1+1/d).
consequence: It is used to flag fabricated accounting data, to design efficient data coding, and to explain why logarithmic scales suit phenomena spanning many decades.

title: The Collatz Conjecture
subject: Number Theory
statement: Halve an even number, or triple an odd one and add 1: the conjecture claims every start eventually reaches 1.
short: A rule you can explain to a child has defeated every proof attempt for more than eighty years.
long: Also called the 3n + 1 problem, this is an open problem, not a theorem. Starting at 27 the orbit wanders above 9000 before falling back to 1 after 111 steps; other starts behave just as erratically. Computers have checked enormous ranges, and Tao proved that almost all orbits eventually dip below any fixed unbounded threshold, but no argument yet shows that every orbit reaches the cycle 4 → 2 → 1.
proof: No proof is known. Computation verifies the claim for enormous ranges; Tao's 2019 theorem shows that almost every orbit dips below any prescribed unbounded threshold, which is still weaker than reaching 1.
consequence: It is the most famous example of a simply stated arithmetic process whose long-term behaviour cannot yet be predicted, and it drives research on iteration and stopping times.

title: The Seven Bridges of Königsberg
subject: History of Mathematics
statement: No walk through Königsberg can cross each of its seven bridges exactly once, even without returning to the start.
short: Euler turned a local puzzle about bridges into the first theorem of graph theory.
long: The Pregel river split Königsberg into four land masses joined by seven bridges, and locals wondered whether a stroll could use each bridge once. Euler's 1736 paper reduced the city to dots and lines and observed that any intermediate land mass needs an even number of bridges: every arrival must be paired with a departure. All four land masses have odd degree, so the walk is impossible. The paper is generally cited as the birth of graph theory.
proof: In a trail using every edge once, every vertex except possibly the two endpoints has even degree. Here the degrees are 3, 3, 5 and 3 — four odd vertices — so no such trail exists.
consequence: It established the habit of modelling a problem by its connectivity alone and led directly to Eulerian paths, circuits and the wider language of graphs.

title: The Continued Fraction for e
subject: Number Theory
statement: The continued fraction of e repeats a striking pattern: 1, 2, 1, 1, 4, 1, 1, 6, 1, 1, 8, …
short: Where π's continued fraction looks random, e's falls into a rhythm you can recite.
long: Euler found in 1737 that after the initial 2, the partial quotients of e arrive in triples (1, 2k, 1) for k = 1, 2, 3, … . This regularity is unique among the famous constants and gives exceptionally good rational approximations: 19/7 and 193/71 are convergents. Because the expansion never terminates, it also certifies at a glance that e is irrational.
proof: Euler's transformation of a series into a continued fraction, applied to e=\sum_{k\ge0}1/k!, gives the pattern (1,2k,1) for k=1,2,3,\dots after the initial 2.
consequence: The pattern proves e is irrational, supplies its best rational approximations, and inspired the search for continued fractions of other constants.

title: The Borwein Integrals
subject: Analysis
statement: Seven sinc factors give exactly π/2; adding an eighth drops the integral by only about 2.3 × 10⁻¹¹.
short: A numerical pattern that looks ironclad for seven terms quietly breaks at the eighth.
long: David and Jonathan Borwein published this in 2001 as a warning about experimental mathematics. The integrals stay at exactly π/2 while the odd denominators 3, 5, … satisfy 1/3 + 1/5 + ⋯ < 1; that partial sum is about 0.955 through 13, but including 15 pushes it past 1. The resulting deficit is so tiny that ordinary numerical integration would miss it entirely.
proof: Each sinc is the characteristic function of a uniform variable on [-a_k,a_k], so the product is that of their sum S. Fourier inversion gives the integral as \pi f_S(0). While \sum_{k\ge1}a_k<a_0=1 the density at 0 is exactly 1/2; including a_7=1/15 breaks that plateau.
consequence: It is a favourite cautionary tale for experimental mathematics and links sinc integrals to random walks, characteristic functions and signal processing.

title: The Kruskal Count
subject: Discrete Mathematics
statement: Two readers following different hidden paths through a shuffled deck usually end on the very same card.
short: A magician can name your final card without knowing your starting card, because the two paths merge.
long: The trick is performed with a shuffled deck whose cards the magician never sees. A spectator secretly picks a starting card and repeatedly jumps forward by that card's value; the magician does the same from an arbitrary start. Once the two paths land on a common card they coincide forever, and with a full deck this coupling happens with overwhelming probability before the deck runs out. Dynkin described the phenomenon in the 1950s; Kruskal rediscovered it as a card trick in the 1970s.
proof: Both paths iterate the same map from different starts; once they meet they merge forever. The chance of avoiding every coincidence position decays exponentially, so the coupling time is usually short compared with the length of the deck.
consequence: Coupling is now a general tool for comparing Markov chains and appears in cryptography, self-synchronising codes and Pollard's kangaroo algorithm for discrete logarithms.

title: 0.999… Equals 1
subject: Recreational Mathematics
statement: The repeating decimal 0.999… is not merely close to 1 — it is exactly equal to 1.
short: Two different decimal strings can name exactly the same real number.
long: Students often feel that 0.999… should be just less than 1, with an infinitesimal gap left over. But a decimal expansion is defined as the limit of its truncations, and those truncations approach 1 with no gap at all. The same phenomenon gives 0.4999… = 1/2 and, more generally, every terminating decimal has a second representation ending in repeating nines.
proof: Let x=0.999\dots . Then 10x-x=9, so x=1; equivalently 9\sum_{n\ge1}10^{-n}=9\cdot(1/10)/(1-1/10)=1.
consequence: It is the standard entry point to limits and infinite series, and to the fact that decimal representation is not unique.

title: Among Six People, a Triangle
subject: Discrete Mathematics
statement: Among any six people there are either three mutual acquaintances or three mutual strangers.
short: Complete disorder is impossible once a group is large enough: some structure must appear.
long: Represent people as vertices and colour each edge red or blue according to whether the pair knows each other. Ramsey's theorem says that a sufficiently large complete graph must contain a monochromatic triangle, and for two colours and triangles the smallest such size is exactly six. The general result guarantees such structured subgraphs for any number of colours and any target shape, though it says nothing about where to find them.
proof: From one vertex, at least three of the five edges share a colour, say red to A,B,C. If any edge among A,B,C is red we have a red triangle; otherwise ABC is blue. Five vertices fail: a red 5-cycle with blue complement has no monochromatic triangle.
consequence: It launched Ramsey theory, the study of unavoidable order in large structures, with links to combinatorics, logic and extremal graph theory.
